lesson_title: The Ball That Will Not Fit
hook_text: A metal ball slips through a ring. Heat it for one minute and it gets stuck on top. Nothing was added. What changed?
clip_script: A brass ball drops neatly through a brass ring. Now heat the ball in a flame for one minute and try again. It sits on top, stuck. Wait a few minutes, and it drops through. Nothing was added, nothing taken away. Inside, the brass particles got more energy and jiggled harder, pushing each other a little further apart. The particles did not grow; the gaps did. The ball got bigger, but its mass stayed the same, so its density fell. That tiny effect is why old railway lines had gaps between rails, why bridges have metal teeth across the road, and why power lines droop. And it is the reason your kettle switches itself off: a strip of two metals inside bends as it heats, because one metal expands more than the other.
visual_style: A whiteboard ball and ring with a flame, then a zoom into jiggling particles with growing gaps, then quick sketches of a rail gap, a bridge joint and a bending bimetallic strip.
pacing: A slow demonstration, then a snappy run of real-world examples.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain expansion with particles.
